title: How an LLM works
description: Follow text from raw tokens into vectors, attention layers, large-scale pretraining, and human alignment.

steps.caption: Text is first broken into small pieces called tokens—words, subwords, or punctuation—so a model can assign each piece an integer ID.
Each token ID is looked up in an embedding table, turning discrete symbols into dense vectors that capture semantic meaning.
Attention lets every token inspect all earlier tokens in the sentence and weigh which context words matter most right now.
Stacking attention and feed-forward blocks creates a Transformer—the parallel architecture behind modern language models.
During pretraining, the model predicts the next token across trillions of words, absorbing grammar, facts, and reasoning patterns.
Supervised fine-tuning adapts the base predictor into a helpful assistant trained on curated instruction-response pairs.
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback shapes the model's tone and helpfulness using human preference rankings.
The result is a Large Language Model: a general-purpose text engine capable of summarizing, coding, translating, and reasoning.

title: NLP from scratch
description: Trace the evolution of Natural Language Processing from classical text cleaning and word counts to modern Transformers.

steps.caption: Early and modern pipelines begin by normalizing text—cleaning noise, handling casing, and standardizing encodings.
Tokenization splits raw character streams into manageable units like words or subwords for downstream modeling.
Bag of Words represents documents as simple word-frequency counts—fast and interpretable, though word order is lost.
Word embeddings placed words in continuous vector space so synonyms sit close together and analogies become vector math.
Sequence models like RNNs and LSTMs restored word order by reading tokens step-by-step and carrying hidden memory.
Transformers replaced slow step-by-step recurrence with parallel self-attention, unlocking long-range understanding.

title: From prompt to answer (RAG)
description: See how Retrieval-Augmented Generation grounds an LLM's response in fresh, external knowledge.

steps.caption: Everything starts with a user prompt—the question, instruction, or task sent into the system.
An embedding model converts the user's question into a numeric vector representing its semantic intent.
A vector database stores millions of document chunks as embeddings and indexes them for fast nearest-neighbor search.
Retrieval fetches the top matching passages whose vectors lie closest to the prompt's query vector.
Those retrieved passages are injected alongside the user's prompt inside the model's context window.
Finally, the model generates an answer conditioned on the retrieved evidence, reducing guesswork and hallucinations.
